FACULTY SENATE OFFICE 224 PASTORE HALL, 51 LOWER COLLEGE ROAD, KINGSTON, RI 02881 USA, P: 401.874.2616 NOVEMBER 7, 2024 Dear Senators, Our community at-large and the faculty senate are both committed to protecting expressive speech as a core right underpinning academic freedom at the University of Rhode Island.
The recent DRAFT University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees Regulations Regarding Use of University Property, if approved without revision, would undermine this right.
It girds an overly vague set of conditions for the use of property with punitive consequences to be administered with vague guidelines and unfettered power.
Despite the inclusion of language which emphasizes learning, the letter makes no specific reference to academic freedom or its prominence in our University Manual (Chapter 6).
In this letter, I summarize the phases of the regulation's evolution over the past several months, as far as I am aware.
Then, I provide a short summary of the major concerns about the regulation that senators and other community members have identified.
Finally, I outline next steps.

Timeline • Spring/Summer 2024: Various communications from the URI administration indicated that lack of a policy pertaining to protest and its potential harms, particularly with respect to university property, was a concern. • Late August 2024: In writing, I requested senate review of policy drafts given potential bearing on academic life.
I received no reply in advance of the below steps. • Early October 2024: The DRAFT regulations were presented to the Administrative Policy Committee (on which I sit as Senate President) by Vice President of Administration and Finance (VPAF) Benson.
The DRAFT regulation was supplied one hour.
I raised concerns about austerity and potential impacts at the meeting, despite having to comment in real-time.
It was posted for public comment by the next day. • Mid-October 2024: Concerns arise in the community following communications to union members by the AAUP-URI executive director. • Late October 2024: Senate leadership meets with the VPAF and her staff.
The parties tentatively agree to participate in an ad hoc committee to assist with redress of the substantive problems, in addition to holding a forum at the next senate meeting.

Process issues about how these policies were shared and not properly vetted will be addressed at a future time.
Major Concerns Many senators have written to me by email or posted comments (400+) to the VPAFs policy site.
Of these, I am attaching four letters from senators and faculty, as well as a comment

written by the Rhode Island ACLU Executive Director and sent to the VPAF on the matter.
At a minimum, the following major areas of concern have been cited as areas of major concern around the proposed regulation. • The need for a policy or regulation to react to protest events on a campus that has essentially never seen violent protest, and which has a tradition of peaceful, participatory, and deliberative discourse, is ostensibly undocumented. • The policy is very vague on how response to property damage events will be pursued.
References to other handbooks, manuals, contracts, and laws seem to have been sufficient to manage any event involving damage to property in the past.

It is not clear how these policies will be enacted differently under this regulation, or if they should be. • Even if the regulation is stood up, there is a seemingly draconian presentation of severe punishments bereft of clear attendant policy, due process, and collective participation of appropriate university bodies. • There is a clear lack of common sense considerations in the regulation, such as faculty not being able to access their labs in off-hours, punishments for simple infractions such as littering with a flyer, and so on. • The forceful, top-down style, in the document and in procedural choices, contrasts starkly with the norms of a community that prides itself on academic freedom, constructive expressive speech, and civility, and with the expectations of a senate that is an equal partner in shared governance.
Charge to Attend and Engage Modern universities should form an intellectually safe, free marketplace of ideas.
Our faculty and students need to be able to express themselves without the weight of oppressive and potentially life altering consequences hanging over their heads while engaging in study, life and work.

This is especially true for our students who are learning to use their voices for change and good.
This DRAFT regulation is clearly not in-line with these imperatives.
Our task is to ensure that these issues are addressed through our deliberations and advocacy, and, if necessary, through legislation.
Please join us at the next Faculty Senate meeting on November 14 at 3:00 PM in the Hope Room, Higgins Welcome Center, at which time this matter will be discussed.
There are other important topics on the agenda, and many people will wish to speak on this matter, so please come prepared with concise statements.
We will not be addressing matters of university and senate process around policies and regulations at this meeting; however, we will be considering this need at another time.
Sincerely, Theodore (Ted) Walls URI Faculty Senate President, 2024-2025

Most of the listed limitations and prohibited activities (2a-2o) look reasonable.

For example, if a student affixes a poster or a sign to the exterior of a building, could s/he face disciplinary action up to termination?
I would say “let them post” and URI employees can pull unauthorized posters later.

What events put this proposal forward?
To the best of my knowledge, we did not have any encampments, or damage to campus property this year.
Is our administration under pressure from donors or politicians?
Conclusion After 13 years at URI, it is clear to me that political violence or destruction of campus property are not big issues in Kingston but on the contrary, it is lack of dissent and weak activism that slows down the growth of our students.

Many URI students have no idea or don’t care about what is going on beyond their small worlds!
Any policy that directly/indirectly discourages (the already weak) campus activism and demonstrations actually hurts the development of our students and I propose that • 2g is removed • The disciplinary actions for other violations be clarified • URI Administration shares with us - why now, justify the need for these restrictions • The introduction paragraph of the document can be extended to underline freedom of speech & assembly as vital elements of academic freedom and that buildings partially serve this purpose.

Thoughts on draft regulations for use of URI property: The draft is very legalistic and very top-down; it is “command-and-control” in tone.
The subtext of the regulations is that misbehavior will not be tolerated.
I’m not sure that is an eCective message to control the members of a University community.
The Introduction does not mention the special role of the University as a place where dissent is protected, and where the interruption of normal activities by peaceful civil disobedience is accepted for its potential contribution to civic discourse and social change.
As a place that honors free speech, the University should project collegiality and respect, even in laying down rules.
Some prohibitions in the draft are unnecessarily granular, treating such things as discarded leaﬂets (litter), impeding traCic, hanging banners, etc., which might occur during demonstrations, as punishable oCences.
History shows that prohibition of minor and incidental acts is often an invitation to law-breaking and/or an excuse to arrest, rather than an eCective way of controlling behavior.

It should also be noted that such prohibitions foster cynicism and undermine the trust of community members in their leaders and their pride in representing the institution.
The option of achieving community peace through consultation and dialogue with parties in conﬂict is not mentioned.
However, this is a far more eCective way to achieve the apparent goals of the draft, without threats and without talking down to the University community.
I recommend that: (1) this draft be revised in a negotiation process involving several sectors of the University community (administrators, staC, faculty, student organizations).
The revision should seek a balance between the administration’s control needs and recognition of the University’s special role in society as a place where dissent is protected; (2) minor, symbolic, and incidental acts be removed from the list of chargeable oCences; and (3) exceptions to the rules laid down be granted either in writing or verbally.

Thomas Zorabedian, Ed.D.
Adjunct Professor, Film/Media and Honors Program Former Assistant Dean, URI College of Arts & Sciences zman@uri.edu RE: Proposed “Regulations Regarding Use of University Property” At its best, a university is a marketplace of ideas.
These ideas may be, and often are, diverse and contradictory, or even at times contentious.
At its weakest, universities discourage or even squelch the free exchange of opinions, beliefs, and feelings.
I recall a time, including specifically at URI, when students and faculty regularly embraced the former approach and engaged in lively interactions.
I fear that the trend in general seems to be in a different direction of less tolerance for public and disparate engagement on campus.
To this end, parts of the proposed regulations raise some concerns that they are not entirely in keeping with the university’s mission which specifically refers to “the freedom to learn” and the “dissemination of new knowledge aimed at contributing to the public good.” Most of the regulations regarding the “control and use” of the university property seem reasonable, sensible, and even innocuous.

Of course, I agree that the destruction, defacing, and vandalizing of property and violation of various laws should be prohibited.
However, two sections include language that could unnecessarily restrict the freedom of expression, and in fact could discourage or even severely punish those who choose to express and share their ideas: 2(f): “Leafletting and Distribution of Literature.” The proposal only allows this time-tested approach “provided that the activity does not impede the flow of pedestrian or vehicular traffic…or create litter.” What exactly does this mean?
Is this a major problem?
While no one should force material on anyone, does going up to someone while they are walking and stopping to give them material “impede” them?
And, if someone who is given some material throws it away, is the person handing it out in violation of littering?
These are not irrelevant questions, because section 3 refers to “suspension or expulsion” as a possible enforcement, a draconian response. 2(g): “Signs, Posters, Banners.” Again, signs that create permanent or temporary damage should not be allowed.

But, could students who attach a sign or drape a banner to a wall, dorm balcony, or building be suspended or expelled, as per section 3?
URI has had innumerable instances over the years of students displaying sentiments or slogans, with the intent of “contributing to the public good,” with no damage to university property.
In fact, the lack of such signage has been conspicuous over the last decade or so.
Further, this section states that “no signs supported by standards or sticks shall be permitted in any assembly inside any building.” If this were a regulation at our country’s national conventions, a good percentage of the attendees would have been thrown out or arrested.
I assume the concern is that a “stick” may become a weapon of some kind.
Obviously, that kind of usage should not be tolerated and should be dealt with harshly.
However, because signs and banners are often held up by some means of support, it follows that the peaceful use of this method of expression should be allowed.
Further, it would be refreshing to see more of this on a campus when students usually seem uninvolved in political, cultural, or social issues.

While I understand that damage to university property can be costly, time-consuming, and aesthetically disagreeable, one of the great and important traditions and freedoms of university life, including at URI, since the late 1960s has been the thoughtful sharing and display of ideas and information.
We should do what we can to encourage that essential aspect of learning, rather than develop new ways to suppress it.
Respectfully submitted, Thomas Zorabedian

Theodore Walls, Faculty Senate President URI Faculty Senate Executive Committee Dear Ted: Per the request of FSEC to provide comments on a proposed University Regulation under consideration by the Senate and the wider URI community, I offer the following observations.
In Section 2 of the proposed regulation there is a listing of Limitations and Prohibited Activities.
In many of these prohibited practices, there is a tacit disregard for the tools by which those with less power within established social hierarchies can express their point of view with enough impact to effectively communicate with powerful decision makers.
As Frederick Douglas once wrote, “Power concedes nothing without a demand.
It never did and it never will.” The University of Rhode Island largely since the Presidency of Francis Horn in the 1960s has strongly embraced a principles of community free speech in opposition of national public policies such as the Vietnam War, and in the late 1970s in response to unfair state labor practices.
Notably, the former provost Beverly Swan (of Swan Hall fame) was a prominent protester staffing the luncheon buffets set up during the high-profile faculty strike.

Moreover, there has been effective protest of university policies that have led to meaningful positive changes at URI.
In the early 1990s, effective protests by the “Brothers United” occupied Taft Hall over civil rights issues and greater emphasis on racial equity at URI.
There was effective communication to President Carothers and the RI Board of Governors for Higher Education that something was very wrong at URI in race relations.
President Carothers then went on to establish the Multicultural Center in the center of campus.
It seems reasonable to prohibit violence or endangerment to others by university regulation, but some other proposed regulations may constitute only a minor nuisance to community members.
These proposed regulations include disruption of meetings, impeding building entry for a while, etc. might be tolerated for a time and resolved by official dialog.
Various other practices listed for possible prohibition could be construed as ordinary vigorous expressions of free speech, including leafleting, signs, posters, banners, erection of structures, camping overnight as part of protest action although a nuisance.
Nuisance is the point!

Why would protesters go through the bother unless they felt something important to say?
Picking up after protesters is not much different than cleaning up after a football game.
The one of the most egregious “Catch 22s” of the proposed regulation is in item o, “Sanitation.
Outdoors” in which defecation or urination is prohibited.
This seems reasonable at first glance, but this item is accompanied by item k, Building Access, where all the restrooms are located.
One might avail of a sanitation company to bring in temporary latrines to service protesters, but this

might be construed as violating item i “Erection of Structures”, requiring permission of the VP. What if the VP is not sympathetic to the cause of the protesters and denies permission to protest? Could the bodily functions be used as a weapon against sustained free speech activities? One of the most prominent non-sequiturs in the proposed regulations is item m, prohibiting bicycles, skateboards and other conveyances on campus. In an era of developing alternatives to fossil fuels, any sort of carbon-free transport to the university from outside and within the university should be encouraged rather than discouraged. Perhaps a joint senate and administration effort to develop vehicular traffic norms around campus may be a more effective strategy of maintaining pedestrian safety. Thank you for this opportunity to comment. Sincerely, Michael A. Rice, PhD Faculty Senator, CELS

COMMENTS ON PROPOSED UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND BOARD OF TRUSTEES REGULATIONS REGARDING USE OF UNIVERSITY PROPERTY October 2024 The American Civil Liberties Union of Rhode Island appreciates the opportunity to offer comments on the Board of Trustees’ proposed regulations regarding University Property . We understand that they are designed to convey the University of Rhode Island’s commitment to quality education through the use and protection of its University Property. Some provisions in these proposed regulations, however, also have a deleterious effect, even if unintentional, on the University’s concomitant commitment to protecting academic freedom and the First Amendment rights of students. It is with the goal of safeguarding those rights that we offer the following comments for consideration. The Proposed Regulations 1. Section 2(a). Individual Rights: This section prevents using University Property “in a manner that impinges upon the rights of another person under the United States or Rhode Island Constitution; any federal, state, or local law; or any University policy.” While one cannot argue with this goal in the abstract, we are concerned about its potential misuse in implementation. On university campuses across the country, we have recently seen conflicts where student speech on political matters is said – often unfairly, in our view – to impinge on the rights of other students to feel safe or free from discrimination. We believe 128 Dorrance Street, Suite 400 Providence, RI 02903 Phone: (401) 831-7171 Fax: (401) 831-7175 www.riaclu.org info@riaclu.org

2 this provision must better define when use of University Property “impinges upon the rights of another person” in order to avoid confusion and disputes about its potential application to unpopular, but constitutionally protected, opinions or speech by either faculty or students. 2.
Section 2(e).
Endangerment: This section prohibits the use of University Property to “endanger” others.
The word “endanger” is undefined, which leaves it open to wide interpretation and, again, potentially applicable to protected speech.
We would urge that the wording be clarified to explicitly refer to physical endangerment. 3.
Section 2(f).
Leafletting and Distribution of Literature: This section would allow the university to bar leafletting or distribution of literature if it “create[s] litter.” This is extremely problematic and should be stricken.
The exercise of free speech rights cannot be prohibited because of the improper behavior of others.
Littering by students who receive a leaflet is out of the control of the distributor, yet this provision would allow for the denial of the leafleteer’s First Amendment rights on the basis of a third party’s actions.
For close to a century, the U.S.

Supreme Court has rejected such efforts.1 Also, while leafletters should not be allowed to block access to buildings or walkways while engaged in this quintessential First Amendment activity, we are concerned that the rule’s ban on “impeding” the flow of pedestrian traffic could be interpreted in an overly restrictive manner.
After all, any distribution of literature has the potential to contribute to temporary bottlenecks, but that should not serve as a basis for prohibiting it. 1 As far back as 1939, the Court noted: “We are of opinion that the purpose to keep the streets clean and of good appearance is insu=icient to justify an ordinance which prohibits a person rightfully on a public street from handing literature to one willing to receive it. . . .
There are obvious methods of preventing littering.
Amongst these is the punishment of those who actually throw papers on the streets.” Schneider v.
State, 308 U.S. 147, 162 (1939).

3 We urge that this wording be modified so as to bar, for exam ple, leafletting only if it “significantly” impedes the flow of traffic.
This section also gives Housing and Residential Life and Dining Services the ability to develop additional leafletting restrictions for areas under their control.
This provision should require those departments to explicitly articulate their rationale for any additional restrictions and ensure that they are narrowly crafted to address the specific issue warranting these extra limitations.
Indeed, from our perspective, one might expect residential facilities at the school to have fewer, not greater, restrictions. 4.
Section 2(g).
Signs, Postings, Banners: This section limits the posting of signs to designated areas of University Property, specifically “designated bulletin boards or other areas identified for positing [sic].” In line with our comments on Section 2(f), we would urge that this be clarified to exempt dormitory rooms and related areas within those buildings.

For example, a student who wishes to display a banner from a window either inside or outside their dorm room, or to post a political sign on their door, should be allowed to do so without fear of punishment.
The University should not have the discretion to determine whether such areas are “designated” for posting signs.
In addition, if the locations that the University “designates” for sign posting are insufficiently prevalent or unduly restrictive, this rule could severely impac t communication between students for purposes of noticing meetings, rallies or other events.
We recommend that the rules provide a process to allow students to formally petition to have a location be deemed a designated area for posting information beyond those set out initially by the University.

4 5.
Section 2(i).
Erection of Structures: This section prohibits erecting both permanent and temporary structures without specific written permission.
The scope of “temporary structures” should be defined and limited.
If a “structure” is erected for a minimum period of time in concert with a political protest or similar activity, written permission should not be required any more than the temporary use of open university space itself for a spontaneous protest or rally.
These situations are very different from the type of encampment concerns that this rule seems to be aimed at , but they would be treated identically as this rule is presently worded. 6.
Section 2(k).
Building Access: This section grants the University the right to ask guests in residential buildings “to leave at any time.” This completely standardless authority to order guests to leave is quite inappropriate.
The policy should have a “good cause” requirement and specify the types of conduct that would authorize the University to remove a guest from a residential building.
A broad “in loco parentis” standard is simply anachronistic and unwarranted in the university setting. 7.
Section 3.

Enforcement and Violations: This section states that violations of any of these policies can result in various disciplinary actions, including the imposition of fines.
The section specifies that the Board of Trustees derives authority to impose fines from RIGL §16-32-2.
However, that statute allows a “district or police court,” not the University, to impose fines for violations of school policies.
Furthermore, under this section, the user of the University Property is deemed responsible for any property damage that is incurred, even if the user did not cause the damage.
For example, if a protest takes place on campus and a counter-protester throws a

5 rock through a window, the organizer – and not the protester who threw the rock – would be held responsible under this section. It should be revised to avoid any such scenario. In sum, the ACLU believes it is important that these rules be revised to be more mindful of their potential impact and infringement on the exercise of First Amendment rights, and that they make clear that they can be applied to speech activity only in accordance with the time, place and manner restrictions appropriate for a public or limited public forum. Thank you for your consideration of our views. We trust that they will be given your careful consideration. Submitted by: Steven Brown, Executive Director American Civil Liberties Union of Rhode Island

1 Faculty Senate Executive Committee Bill #2026-2027-01 1 September 17, 2026 Faculty Senate Meeting - INTRODUCTION ONLY 2 Creates standard process for committee formation 3 Approved by FSEC 08/31/26 4 Approved by CBUM XX/XX/XX 5 6 Legislation effective date: Spring semester 2027 7 8 Rationale: The limited number of faculty senators, in combination with University-9 Manual-mandated committee staffing requirements, can make it difficult to staff an expanding 10 number of standing committees.
This makes it important to ensure that additional standing 11 committees, whose charges and memberships are proscribed in the University Manual, are 12 created only in response to a significant and sustained need.
In contrast, special committees can 13 be created by the Faculty Senate to address pressing issues.

While there is no limit to the length 14 of time a special committee can exist, the faculty senate must vote to reauthorize each special 15 committee each year. 16 This legislation mandates that a newly formed committee must exist as a special 17 committee for at least three (3) years before legislation reconstituting it as a standing committee, 18 subcommittee, or joint committee can be considered by the Faculty Senate.
Such legislation must 19 be accompanied by language specifying the charge and membership of the standing committee 20 for inclusion in the University Manual.
This change provides time for the Faculty Senate to 1) 21 consider whether a new standing committee, subcommittee, or joint committee is truly 22 warranted; and 2) craft an appropriate and achievable charge for the body. 23 This legislation does not mandate that a special committee must be reconstituted as a 24 standing committee after three years.

Creating a faculty- and 128 student-representative-only Committee on Online and Distance Learning would require the 129 formation of a special faculty committee tasked with bringing forward legislation establishing 130 such a body. 131 Detailed response to amendment proposed at 5/7/26 meeting: 132 Rationale for Maintaining Joint Voting: The proposed revision of the membership 133 structure is designed to preserve JCODL as a meaningful joint governance body while ensuring 134 strong faculty leadership and representation. 135 Faculty hold a majority of the voting membership.

The remaining voting membership includes four 140 institutional representatives whose areas have direct responsibility for the delivery and support of 141 online and distance education, as well as graduate and undergraduate student representatives. 142 This structure protects a strong faculty role in academic governance while recognizing 143 that the work of JCODL also intersects with institutional responsibilities for the delivery and 144 support of online education.
The institutional members do not participate solely as technical 145 resources; they represent areas with direct responsibility for implementing and supporting 146 matters within the committee’s charge.
Their voting participation allows those responsibilities 147 and faculty academic perspectives to be considered as recommendations are developed. 148 The proposed structure also deliberately distinguishes between voting membership and ex 149 officio participation.

Two senior administrators may participate as non-voting ex officio 150 members.
This demonstrates that the proposed structure does not assume that every administrator 151 connected to online education requires a vote.
Rather, voting membership is limited to the 152 faculty, students, and institutional roles identified as core participants in the committee’s work. 153 Joint Voting and Faculty Authority: Maintaining voting participation by institutional 154 members does not diminish Faculty Senate authority.
JCODL is an advisory and recommending 155 body.
Under the proposed §5.78.11, it provides advice and guidance to both the Provost and 156 Faculty Senate and consults appropriate committees, units, and personnel. 157 Matters requiring Faculty Senate approval continue through Faculty Senate governance, 158 while matters requiring administrative authority remain subject to the appropriate administrative 159 processes.

Joint voting therefore allows JCODL to develop informed recommendations through 160 meaningful participation by both faculty and institutional representatives without changing 161 where final authority resides. 162 Governance Consideration: If there is interest in changing JCODL from a Joint 163 Committee of the Faculty Senate and the President to a Faculty Senate committee, that represents 164 a broader governance question concerning the status and purpose of the committee. 165 Making the institutional members non-voting would materially alter the joint governance 166 structure proposed in Bill 2025-2026-09.
